Fungal infections in immunocompromised patients are of- ten invasive or disseminated and treatment should start as early as possible. A fungal cause of infection should be considered in patients with persistent febrile neutropenia who have not responded to broad spectrum antibacterials. If the infection has not been identified, empirical treatment should be started. Conventional intravenous amphotericin B has been considered first-line empirical therapy and is no less effective than lipid formulations. Fluconazole, itra- conazole, voriconazole, and caspofungin appear at least as effective as amphotericin B. For patients with renal im- pairment lipid formulation of amphotericin B or voricona- zole may be given. For patients not responding to an am- photericin B formulation voriconazole, itraconazole, or caspofungin are alternatives. Fluconazole may be consid- ered for low risk patients infected with susceptible Candi- da species. The benefit and role of primary prophylaxis in the man- agement of fungal infections associated with HIV, cancer, and organ transplants is controversial as this may select for resistant isolates and species not susceptible to the antifun- gals used. This is of particular concern with fluconazole (see Resistance, p.533 ), one of the drugs most widely used for this purpose. Fluconazole has been shown to be effec- tive as primary prophylaxis against invasive candidiasis but not aspergillosis. Itraconazole or voriconazole are pre- ferred for patients at risk of invasive aspergillosis, such as patients being treated for graft-versus-host disease or cy- tomegalovirus disease. Long term suppressive therapy has been recommended for immunocompromised patients with proven or probable in- vasive aspergillosis or candidiasis. Secondary prophylaxis may be stopped when patients are no longer profoundly neutropenic. Antifungals are also used in selective digestive tract de- contamination (see Intensive Care, p.175). Treatment and prophylaxis of specific fungal infections in immunocompromised patients is discussed under the ap- propriate headings—see Aspergillosis, Candidiasis, Coc- cidioidomycosis, Cryptococcosis, and Histoplasmosis (above), and Pneumocystis Pneumonia (below).
